prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map supports a coarse layout of a workbench along the upper/front edge, open floor below it, and the camera wearer’s torso, legs, and intermittently extended arm in the near foreground. The wearer’s body and hand appear closest, roughly 0–1 m away; the stool, cart, cables, and bench edge are about 1–2 m away, while the wall, windows, and rear bench area are roughly 2–4 m away. Across the five frames, the viewpoint turns and tilts around the workstation, shifting the nearer bench and body regions laterally rather than showing a clear approach or retreat; no separate person is clearly visible. Compared with RGB, brightness makes near-versus-far surfaces and partial occlusion by the wearer’s body easier to distinguish, but exact metric distances, thin cables, reflective surfaces, frame boundaries, and some bright edge regions look unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates several visible parts of the camera wearer as person instances, including the torso and legs across the lower foreground and an arm or hand extending upward in some frames; these regions are within roughly 0–1 m of the camera. It does not meaningfully segment the bench, stool, cart, tools, cables, floor, or walls, so their positions and separations must still be inferred from RGB; the main layout is a bench ahead and toward the left, with floor objects roughly 1–2 m in front of or beside the wearer. The wearer’s limbs partly occlude the floor and nearby equipment, and some masks continue beyond the lower or side image boundaries, showing that those body parts are partly out of view. Across the frames, the masks reveal changes in the wearer’s visible body outline and an arm rising or extending, but fragmented labels, multiple masks for one wearer, and occasional tiny or misplaced person regions make instance count and precise boundaries unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only sparse magenta hand skeletons, most clearly a hand around the right-middle area in frame 4 and a raised hand near the upper-right in frame 5; both correspond to the camera wearer’s nearby hands, approximately 0.3–1 m from the camera. Their changing image position shows the hand moving upward and farther right relative to the wearer’s viewpoint, with the final hand above the nearby bench surface and partly surrounded by objects visible in RGB. No dependable body skeleton or skeleton for another person is present, so this map does not establish body orientation, gaze direction, inter-person distance, or whether anyone faces the camera wearer. Compared with RGB, it makes detected finger/hand configuration and the hand’s relative location explicit, but it misses most visible limbs and hands in the first three frames and therefore looks incomplete and unreliable for full-body reach or occlusion analysis.
